questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Personal connection to the destination (heritage / friends there/ etc.)

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: The academic opportunities and prospects of going abroad at St Andrews seemed great, as University of St Andrews is listed as one of the most renowned universities in Great Britain. Moreover, I have British family connections and wanted to explore both Scotland and England whilst improving my written and oral English.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: I was really happy about my exchange in St Andrews, especially due to my choice of accommodation at Deans Court, which proved to be a crucial addition to my stay because I gained many friends and connections there who were current master’s and PhD students. This meant they were generally older and more on wavelength than bachelor students.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: So much help. They have a great student service. I got relocated to Deans Court because I couldn’t afford DRA, and in the beginning, they said no but changed their stance. They helped me a lot getting the electives I needed and proved great support when I had a potentially unsettling situation with a future peer (which proved to be perfectly fine in the end, it was just a person I was going to live with, and the student services were invaluable and supportive). They physically helped me find my accommodation and made sure I could borrow bed linen for a few days before I sorted it out and got some for free via St and ReUse. Also, Andrew is a sweetheart, he’s the janitor at Deans and just lovely.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: Hmm, like Powell, DRA, and such.. The Grange and Deans Court are great, also heard alright things about the other halls. But be aware that places like DRA and Fife Park are quite a long walk away, which is annoying when everything is situated quite closely in the centre in such a small town as St Andrews.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: I had a catered accommodation and honestly that was great. Only option at Deans. It gives you so much for time to study, and the supermarkets in St Andrews are incredibly expensive anyway

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: Can recommend finding a place early either on the Facebook pages (but watch out for scammers!!) or find it via their system. But it is quite expensive via the university... And if you want to live in university housing, do your research well! Because it varies a lot - although this REALLY goes for the facebook groups as well... I got into a nasty situation with a guy on Facebook, so I can recommend starting your housing search early so you don't get into a desperate situation.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Deans court isn’t usually available for exchange students. But they made an exception because somebody didn’t want the spot anyway in august. Usually, you get allocated a spot mid-July and have to accept or decline. And when people decline, spots open up around August.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: Everything is in-person, so quite easy actually. I was stressing a lot about it before-hand but it proved out to be quite ok. But go the the academic fayres in September (start of term), because in this way you get to  chat to the teachers about their subjects etc.. It's just a lot of e-mailing and admin back and forth, honestly.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: You get appointed a personal supervisor for academic advising, who helps you choose your subjects. So its really quite practical.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Got all the classes I wanted.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Trust in the process! All the admin work will pay off and calm down - just get it over and done with, so it's not hanging over your head all the time. And ask the university for help, if you need it. They're really friendly in the adminstration.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Honestly, it wasn't the academic programmes I learned the most from... Maybe the experience in general. And then the assignments - in total we had to write 45-50 academic English pages throughout the semester (before mid-December, when the term officially ends). So it was quite busy, but you only have around 6 hours of class a week.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
CO4038 - Environmental Imaginations (level 4000 bachelor 4-års studerende)
SA5020 - Anthropology, Art and Perception 1 (master level 5000)
CO4034 - Utopia: Past, Present, Futures  (level 4000 bachelor 4-års studerende)

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: More formal. I was not that academically challenging, honestly... It was mostly the big amount of work you had to do, which was quite stressful. At UCPH we're used to writing our exams in January, and here, the exams are written throughout the semester.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
CO4038 - Environmental Imaginations (level 4000 bachelor 4-års studerende)
SA5020 - Anthropology, Art and Perception 1 (master level 5000)
CO4034 - Utopia: Past, Present, Futures  (level 4000 bachelor 4-års studerende)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I wish I had gone for some teachers I had heard good things about, or courses such as: R4572 - Economy of Anger: Marxism, Psychoanalysis and the Politics of Status and SD4118 - Extractive Environments.
Because really, it's more about the teacher than the specific subject. Because they influence the subject so much
Mattia is lovely in Anthropology, Art and Perception, but he's style of teaching kind of sucks and is extremely vague and fluffy. 
Damiano Benvegnu is also kind of Meh... But I liked Nial Sreenan (Utopia)!
I would recommend 'auditing' subjects as well, which you can request to do. Basically just following a course without taking the exams and being officially inscribed.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer:
Costs are extremely high!
Cost of housing: easily 7500-10.000 - mine was 40.000 total for 3,5 months in catered accommodation :O 
Supermarket prices are super high
Cost of balls etc are easily 50 pounds, and it's also quite expensive to join societies and activities

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Same as above. Everything was more expensive...

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Honestly, everything your heart desires. Huge tradition for societies and clubs at Andrews

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Loved "Caledonian Society" - Dancing Scottish Reels once a week
Violin lessons at Laidlaw Music Centre with Gordon
St Leonard's chapel choir 
Debate nights with the Tories
Breakaway hillwalking club
Mountaineering club
Going to church once in a while in a cloak (sooo many beautiful churches)
Clay Pigeon shooting for people watching the rich (but it's a rip-off) 
join the balls even if they're expensive!

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Going on trips to the highlands - Isle of Skye, Fort William, etc.
Join trips via Breakaway or Mountaineering Club

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy, although it's quite conservative which you have to be prepared for

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer:
Join everything you can, and say yes to all the possibilities in the first few weeks. And then see what you like.
Most importantly, go to the academic/sports fayres, and give-it-a-go lessons at the societies.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Many Americans and many privileged people... Especially the bachelor students. Usually, the master's students are a little older (21-35 ish) and have had to work or be on fully paid scholarships in order top afford a master's, which means the master's and PhDs are usually a little older. So can actually really recommend going here as part of a master's exchange, if you're considering it.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I liked the respect for traditions, the Britishness, and observing the weird conservativeness. The cloaks! Coming from a very leftist and communal life here in Copenhagen, it was a cultural shock for sure but I really did enjoy parts of it!

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1) It's pricey. If you can't afford it, think whether you'd rather go to another country where you can receive Erasmus money. Even when trying to save money, with SU and scholarships (13,500) DKK) I ended up spending 25K extra.
2) Take time to find a good place to live! It matters a lot, I think... At least it did for me.
3) Join all the societies and activities you can. That's what made it worthwhile for me. And then ask for extensions for assignments, lol.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Utilise StAndReuse and the charity shops to get things such as duvets, sheets, towels, plates etc.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The general dedication throughout the whole campus! Everybody, from staff to students were just incredibly dedicated to making it a good and worthwhile experience both academically and socially. I think that's what you get from being at a privileged and Ivy-league-ish institution, honestly... It's both really nice and slightly depressing.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer:
I was sick for 3 weeks during my stay and had to go to the doctor's 6 times because of different infections:// so remember to sign up for the doctor's! It's free in St Andrews, and so is prescription medicine, which is helpful.
And the academic stress as well from the assignments! The best advice is to just suck it up, write them and pull and few all-nighters if you have to. There's honestly so much work and it's just part of the experience. You learn a lot from it though!

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
